title: Like leaves
hookLine: Marcus recalls Homer: the generations of people are like leaves in the wind (Meditations 10.34)
last: SHOW IT BY WHAT IT PRODUCES.

cards: Walk down any street in autumn. The leaves come down in the wind, a few at a time, then all at once. You kick through them.

By next spring the same trees will be full again, and none of the new leaves will know about the old ones. Now think about the people who were well-known when your grandparents were young. The names everyone knew.
How many could you name? Marcus kept a few lines from one of the oldest poems in Greek, and he turned to them to remember something about fame, and loss, and time.

teach.b: The lines come from Homer's Iliad. In the middle of the war at Troy, two warriors meet on the battlefield, and one asks the other who he is. The other answers, more or less: why ask about my family?
The generations of people are like leaves.

teach.h: THE WIND SCATTERS, THE FOREST GROWS.
teach.b: The wind scatters some on the ground, and the forest, when spring comes, grows others. So it is with people: one generation grows, another passes away.

In Book Ten, Marcus says that for someone who has taken in the truth, even a short, familiar line like this is enough to free them from grief and fear. Then he applies it, one by one. Your children are leaves.
The people who cheer you, and the ones who curse you or sneer behind your back, leaves. The people who will carry your name and reputation after you're gone, leaves too.
All come in spring, the wind brings them down, and the forest grows others in their place. That's heavy to hear. Marcus had buried several of his own children.
He isn't saying they didn't matter. He's saying how to hold what matters: with open hands. Leaves aren't worthless because they fall.
All summer they feed the tree. Each one is beautiful in its season. It just doesn't last forever, and it was never meant to.
Praise, insult, even fame after death, all leaves.
What's left is how you live this season. Your line: hold it with open hands.

how: Readers of Marcus often use short lines like this one, from poets and philosophers, as reminders of how briefly things last, to loosen the grip of praise, blame and fear.

o: people and fame come and go, so hold them loosely
people bend with life's winds but never break
fame after death makes a life last forever

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: where the leaves line comes from
scatters some leaves on the ground

s: the leaves image is Marcus's own invention
it comes from Homer's Iliad, which Marcus quotes in Book Ten.
Marcus says a short familiar line can free you from grief and fear
for someone who has taken in the truth, he says, even a brief line is enough.
Marcus says the people we love don't matter
he'd buried several children. he's saying how to hold what matters: with open hands.

games.q: you're a warrior at Troy, and an enemy asks about your family line. what does Homer's warrior say first?
o: why ask? people are like leaves.
games.why: he says the generations are like leaves: the wind scatters them, and the forest grows new ones. then he tells his story anyway.

practice: If you can, look out a window or step outside and find leaves, grass, or even a plant on a shelf; if you can't, picture a tree in the wind. Watch it move: some leaves hold, some fall, and nothing is wrong.
Let your breath move with it.

wordCard.voice: Like leaves. Marcus recalls Homer: people come and go like leaves in the wind, and the forest grows new ones in the spring. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: leaves. from Homer's line comparing the generations of people to leaves.

carryVoice: Your line: hold it with open hands. Every leaf still feeds the tree in its season. That's day two hundred seventeen.
